name: Denominator neglect
statement: Offered a 1-in-10 chance and a 7-in-100 chance at the same prize, a large minority take the second, and say they know the odds are worse.
meaning: A probability written as a ratio has two numbers in it, and the claim is that people read the top one and skim the bottom. Two separate experiments carry the name and they answer different questions. In the equal-ratio version, 1 in 10 is set against 10 in 100 and the ratios match, so the only defensible answer is indifference and any preference is a curiosity rather than an error. In the unequal version the large bowl is strictly worse, 7 red beans in 100 against 1 in 10, and choosing it costs the chooser money. Only the second is a mistake in the ordinary sense, and the two are routinely reported as one result. Reyna and Brainerd's review is the usual source for a mechanism, but only its abstract was read here, and that abstract offers fuzzy-trace theory rather than any account of classes nested one inside the other. It does credit the description of denominator neglect to themselves and, independently, to Epstein, whose group worked the same effect under the name ratio bias. The health version drops the bowls. Risks quoted per 10,000 people are rated as larger than the same risks quoted per 100, which is where any policy interest in the effect lives.

origin.who: L. A. Kirkpatrick and Seymour Epstein
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Three experiments on 1,331 people had participants choose between two bowls offering equivalent chances stated with different absolute numbers, such as 1 in 10 against 10 in 100. The paper is closed at the publisher and only its abstract was read, from Europe PMC on 21 September 2026. Denes-Raj and Epstein's jelly-bean study, the one everybody cites, came two years later and made the large bowl strictly worse. Lefebvre's group trace the paradigm back to Miller, Turnbull and McFarland in 1989, on how suspicious a coincidence feels. Passerini's group, and a footnote in Dale's paper, trace it further, to Piaget and Inhelder's two-urn task with children in 1975. Neither of those was opened during this check.

evidence: Denes-Raj and Epstein paid participants $1 for each red jelly bean drawn and let them pick their bowl. Their abstract reports that people often took the bowl holding more red beans and a smaller share of them, 7 in 100 against 1 in 10, and said afterwards that they knew the odds were against them but felt they had a better chance with more red beans on show. The rates usually quoted, 61% taking the large bowl at 9 in 100 and 40% at 7 in 100, are not read off that paper here. Both figures come from Dale, Rudski, Schwartz and Smith describing it, and Lefebvre, Vieider and Villeval give a range of 54% to 61% for the 9-in-100 case. Dale's group put the effect on a computer and ran it 300 rounds deep on 171 students across six sessions, with the large urn better in some rounds and worse in others. One participant was dropped as an outlier and the tests rest on 162 subject averages per condition. When the large urn was worse, participants chose correctly 59.0% of the time. When it was better, they chose correctly 75.5%. That gap is the bias, and the 25% error rate in the easy direction is the reason the older studies overstate it. The one within-subject test of incentive compared the two sessions paying 10 cents a red marble for half their rounds and nothing for the other half, and accuracy was better in the paid half, t(54) = 2.90, p = .0054. The paper's discussion states plainly that the bias itself was not reduced by incentive. In health framing, Bonner and Newell gave 48 Australian undergraduates eleven causes of death a week apart, once per day and once per year. Every cause scored higher risk in the year frame, mean 14.53 against 13.23 on a 26-point scale, F(1, 45) = 6.17, p = .017, and 30 of the 48 rated the year version higher. The sharpest health figure in this literature is Yamagishi's, and it arrives here through Bonner and Newell and through Lefebvre's group, both of whom report that his participants rated cancer as riskier described as killing 1,286 people out of 10,000 than as killing 24.14 out of 100. Yamagishi's paper was not opened during this check.

examples.text: One barrel holds one winning ticket in ten, the other seven winners in a hundred. A large minority reach into the barrel with seven winners in it, and many of them will say out loud that the odds there are worse.

examples.tag: The risk quoted per ten thousand
examples.text: A leaflet saying a side effect strikes ten people in every ten thousand reads as more alarming than the same risk written as one in a thousand. Nothing about the risk has changed except the size of the numbers describing it.

examples.tag: Two raffle stalls side by side
examples.text: A stall advertising twenty prizes across two thousand tickets draws a longer queue than one offering two prizes across a hundred, though the second is the better bet by a factor of two. The top number is read first.

replication.headline: The standard task reproduces at 68% to 75% across three countries, and falls to chance once the leading sentence goes, an indifference option is added, or real money is paid in randomised order.
replication.detail: Baumeister, Streicher and Lermer ran six studies on 1,338 students in Germany, Turkey and Italy, all with a prize attached, all choosing between 1 in 10 and 10 in 100. The split ran by discipline rather than by country. Social science students took the large urn 74.5%, 75.0%, 68.2%, 73.3% and 71.2% of the time in Studies 2 to 6, while science and engineering students took it 24.3%, 35.2%, 26.7%, 29.4% and 22.6% of the time. Study 1, the only one with real urns on a table and an experimenter present, found 53.4% and 47.3%, close to a coin toss in both groups. Berlin Numeracy Test score predicted the choice in Study 6 regardless of discipline, estimate -0.49, p = 0.025, and Cognitive Reflection Test score did not. Lefebvre, Vieider and Villeval attacked the paradigm as economists. Their first experiment, on 166 volunteers at Erasmus University Rotterdam with the eight choices laid out in order on one page, found 68% taking the large urn at equal odds and 23% still taking it at 9 in 100. Their second experiment gave 78 students in Lyon real money on every decision, up to a 120 euro prize, randomised the order of the pairs and the position of the urns, and added control pairs where the large urn was better. The large urn was chosen 47% of the time at equal odds, indistinguishable from 50%, p = 0.33. When it was worse it was chosen 7.19% of the time against a 9.61% error rate in the opposite direction, t(77) = -0.47, p = 0.64. They conclude the bias is an artefact of uncontrolled error, demand effects and weak incentives. Passerini, Macchi and Bagassi went after the wording instead. Every classic vignette contains a sentence telling participants that the proportions are identical and that they may nonetheless feel one is likelier, and most offer no way to answer 'no preference'. Their strongest lottery condition combined three changes, removing that sentence, adding the third option and replacing the question, and it raised objective answers from the participant's own point of view from 45% to 90% before the outcome and from 39% to 91% after it, chi-squared 14.8 and 18.09, Bonferroni p < .00125. Removing the sentence on its own did almost as much, 45% to 87%, while adding the option on its own did nothing. Their control versions reproduced the originals first.

study.cite: Baumeister, J., Streicher, B., & Lermer, E. (2025). Ratio bias across cultures and disciplines: How academic background shapes statistical decision-making. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 38(1), e70010.

limits: Almost every number here was produced by a student. Dale used Muhlenberg College, one American liberal arts college, Lefebvre used Rotterdam and Lyon, Passerini used 665 Italian undergraduates whose university her paper never names, Baumeister used universities in Germany, Turkey and Italy, and Bonner and Newell used 48 undergraduates at the University of New South Wales. No meta-analysis of ratio bias or denominator neglect was located. Crossref queries on all three phrasings on 21 September 2026 returned the Reyna and Brainerd review, the Szaszi paper, a handbook chapter on reducing denominator neglect and two cardiology letters using the term for something else, and web searches added nothing, so the largest single body of evidence remains Baumeister's 1,338 participants. Three of the founding papers are closed at their publishers and were read only as abstracts: Kirkpatrick and Epstein, Denes-Raj and Epstein, and Reyna and Brainerd's review, which is a synthesis rather than a report of new experiments. Lefebvre's figures were read from the working paper, IZA discussion paper 4546 of November 2009, in the HAL deposit. That is not the article. The published abstract in Theory and Decision differs from the working paper's in its wording, and the published text itself is closed, so nothing here should be taken as checked against the 2011 version. The designs also force a choice. Most of these tasks give two buttons and no way to say the options are the same, and Baumeister's own discussion names that as a limit and asks whether the effect survives without it. Passerini's Experiment 4 is the direct test: about half her control participants said unprompted that they had no preference and were choosing only because they had to.
misreadings: The two paradigms are not one finding. Preferring 10 in 100 to 1 in 10 costs nothing, because the two are the same bet, and a preference between identical options is not an error in probability. Preferring 7 in 100 to 1 in 10 is an error, and it is the rarer and harder result to obtain. Second, nobody in the jelly-bean study was fooled about the odds. The paper's abstract records that participants knew the probabilities were against them and chose anyway, which makes the effect a story about acting against a belief rather than about failing to compute one. Third, Dale's abstract says an incentive significantly reduces irrationality, and its discussion says the ratio bias itself was not reduced by incentive. The first sentence is the one that gets quoted. Fourth, a low rate of large-urn choices is not proof of good reasoning. Baumeister's science and engineering students picked the small urn roughly three times in four when the two urns were identical, which is a systematic preference in the other direction. Fifth, the pull on attention and the mistake in the answer come apart. Szaszi and colleagues stripped the task to bare number pairs and tracked the mouse: on trials where the small ratio was larger, the first movement went to the correct side only 45% and 43% of the time in two experiments, while final accuracy held at 84% and 85%, the same as on easy trials. Finally, this is not base-rate neglect, where the missing number is a prior rather than a denominator, and not insensitivity to sample size, where the neglected quantity is how many observations a result rests on. Both have their own entries. Nor is it proportion dominance, which reverses the complaint: there the denominator is attended to and the absolute number of lives saved is the quantity that goes missing.
